questions.q: What question is the role hierarchy actually designed to answer?
options: Who automatically inherits visibility into whose records
Who reports to whom on the official org chart
Which objects a profile can see at all
Which fields a user can edit on a record
questions.explain: The role hierarchy's only job is to determine upward record visibility. It often resembles the org chart, but an architect designs it around the visibility question specifically, even when that means diverging from the literal reporting structure.

questions.q: A role has no users assigned to it, but sits between two other roles in the hierarchy tree. What is true about this role?
options: It is automatically deleted by Salesforce since it serves no purpose
It grants nobody anything directly, but can still serve a structural purpose controlling how visibility aggregates upward
It blocks all visibility from flowing between the roles above and below it
It automatically inherits the permissions of the nearest role that does have users
questions.explain: A role with zero users grants no one visibility by itself, since visibility only activates once users are placed in a role — but it can still be a useful placeholder that shapes how visibility aggregates for the roles connected to it.

questions.q: OWD for Opportunity is set to Private. A Sales Director role sits above an Account Executive role in the hierarchy, and Grant Access Using Hierarchies is enabled for Opportunity. What does the Sales Director see?
options: Only Opportunities the Sales Director personally owns, since Private OWD overrides the role hierarchy
Nothing extra, because role hierarchy visibility only applies when OWD is Public Read Only or looser
Every Opportunity owned by, or shared with, every Account Executive beneath them in the hierarchy
Only Opportunities explicitly shared through a sharing rule, not through the hierarchy itself
questions.explain: Role hierarchy visibility is a standing structural grant layered on top of OWD, regardless of how restrictive OWD is. A Private OWD doesn't block the role hierarchy from granting upward visibility — it works independently of, and on top of, the OWD baseline.

questions.q: Why does this course recommend a 'wide and shallow' role hierarchy design over one role per management layer?
options: Salesforce technically forbids hierarchies deeper than three levels
Wide and shallow hierarchies are required for Public Read/Write objects specifically
Role depth has no actual effect on performance, only on how the tree looks visually
Deep hierarchies increase sharing recalculation cost and administrative overhead without necessarily matching real visibility needs
questions.explain: Every added level of role hierarchy increases the scope of sharing recalculation when roles or role assignments change, and mirroring every management layer tends to produce far more roles than the actual visibility requirements justify.

questions.q: A regional VP of Sales and an HR Business Partner both report to the same COO two levels up on the real org chart. Why might an architect deliberately give them separate branches in the role hierarchy instead of a shared ancestor role close to the top?
options: Because mirroring the literal chart with a shared nearby ancestor could grant the VP of Sales unintended visibility into HR data through upward role-hierarchy inheritance
Because Salesforce doesn't allow two different departments to share any ancestor role
Because the role hierarchy can only ever be exactly as deep as the real org chart
Because HR records can never participate in a role hierarchy at all
questions.explain: If Grant Access Using Hierarchies is on (the default for standard objects, and common for sensitive custom objects too unless deliberately turned off), putting both roles under one nearby shared ancestor would let that ancestor's access reach both branches, which could leak HR visibility to a Sales-side role that has no legitimate need to see it.
